=== claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players.md
# If every concussion were caught and managed strictly, about one in five players would be out at any time
**What it is** — A back-of-envelope availability model. The speaker, using the survey figure that about half of athletes have a concussion each year, takes a 50-person football team with half concussed (25 players) and 10 days out each: 250 days, "about 4% of playing days", "not completely disruptive" (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]). The speaker then argues recovery is longer than 10 days (see the vulnerability-window entry) and reruns it at 60 days out: "21% of playing days", "one out of five athletes out at all times", about four of a football team's starters and one hockey starter at any moment, not counting repeat concussions (npgdKKdJSww [13:43], [14:14]). The speaker's conclusion is that either medical guidelines get much looser ("which won't happen") or the games "dramatically change" (npgdKKdJSww [14:45], [22:58]). His proposed first step, cutting hitting in practice, comes earlier in the talk (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]).
The speaker says the math was done "on the plane" and that the science is iffy (paraphrase of auto-caption) on the 10-day figure (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]).
**Why it works** — It is arithmetic on three assumed inputs: incidence, days out, and playing days in a season. The speaker gives the first two and not the third. Inference: 250 days equal 4% only if the team has about 6,250 player-days (50 players over about 125 days), and the 60-day case then gives 1,500 days over 6,250, or 24%, not the 21% the speaker states; the two figures are not exactly proportional and the denominator is not shown. Treat both as rough.
**When to apply** — As a reminder to test a proposed detection or return-to-play standard against roster availability before adopting it: ask what the standard would cost in player-days if applied to every case.
Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's role in return to performance is to supply information that supports Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance decisions (Explicit, Playbook p.6), and Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q22): "We don't assess readiness. The template answers that." (Explicit). Inference: an availability estimate like this one is the kind of information Applied Performance could supply; the clearance standard itself stays with Athletic Medicine.
**When NOT to apply** — Do not use the 4% or 21% figures as estimates for Baylor or for any real team. The 50% incidence is a survey figure from the speaker's other studies; the 10-day and 60-day recoveries are assumptions, and the 60-day case is the speaker's hypothetical of what very sensitive tests might demand, not a clinical standard. The model ignores repeat concussions, position differences and substitutions. It is a 2012 talk, and the speaker discloses a consultant role and a test-owner tie (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]).
**Example** — The speaker's own: a 50-person football team, 25 concussed, 60 days out each, "four guys out on your football team every week out of your starting group" (npgdKKdJSww [14:14]).
**Related** — [[claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates]] (source of the 50% input); [[claim--concussion-vulnerability-window-longer-than-return-rules-assumed]] (source of the 30 to 60 day input); [[claim--practice-contact-is-the-largest-exposure-lever-in-football]] (the lever the speaker proposes in response).
=== claim--rule-degrades-when-the-prize-is-worth-as-much-as-the-playoffs.md
# The Rule Does Worse When the Prize Is Worth About as Much as the Playoffs
**What it is** — Evan Monroe tries to "break the rule" with a year when a star prospect (named in the captions as Patrick Ewing) is so valuable that the pick is worth about as much as making the playoffs (-6pe_zOKCig [18:01], [18:31]). The rest of the talk assumes the playoffs are worth more than the pick, which lets many games count (-6pe_zOKCig [18:31]). In the stress case the incentives to lose are high, only the first hundred games count, and the Pacers get the pick with the highest probability but only 19 percent, "not as drastic" as the other case (-6pe_zOKCig [18:31], [19:01]). In Q&A, asked how sensitive the model is to the value of the playoffs versus the pick, he says it is very sensitive around one (equal values; going from one to two) and flat once the ratio is three, four or five (-6pe_zOKCig [25:06]). To set it in practice he suggests data work: first-round pick sale values and how a team's fortunes (TV revenue and so on) change with making the playoffs; the rule only needs a lower bound, and if the true ratio is above the number put into the rule, tanking is not encouraged (-6pe_zOKCig [25:37]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's reason: when the prize is very valuable, incentives to lose are strong, so the rule can use fewer games and the probability distribution cannot be as skewed (-6pe_zOKCig [18:31], [19:01]). He gives no further analysis in the talk.
**When to apply** — As a check on any incentive-based design: vary the assumed relative value of the two goals and report where results change fast. Inference: no direct link found.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one stress case and an oral sensitivity statement, no table or numbers shown beyond 19 percent and the ratio ranges. The bound argument (a lower bound on playoff value is enough) is the speaker's assertion. The stress case is a simulation; the year is only named in captions as a player, so which season it was is not stated in the talk. Do not apply to leagues or sports with different prize structures.
**Example** — The speaker's own: the star-prospect year, where the team with the highest odds under the rule (the Indiana Pacers) gets only 19 percent (-6pe_zOKCig [19:01]).
**Related** — [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]]; [[case-study--1989-miami-heat-back-test-of-the-time-dependent-lottery]].
=== claim--salary-cost-of-ucl-rehab-2004-2014.md
# About Half a Billion Dollars of MLB Salary Went to UCL Rehab, 2004 to 2014
**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]). (Untested: bare assertion, no method given.)
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]). (Untested: back-of-envelope, unadjusted.)
**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.
**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.
**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Inference: MLB dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.
**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).
**Related** — [[claim--ucl-reconstruction-return-outcomes-mlb-pitchers]] (the cohort data that goes with these costs).
=== claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points.md
# Simulated Result: Tree-Search Selection Cut Injuries at Similar Expected Points
**What it is** — The presenters compared their search-based selection with a greedy baseline that picks the team maximizing expected points for each match only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42], [10:12]). They ran thousands of simulations per season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:43], [11:14]). Reported: Brighton would have benefited most, with 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least, with 7.5% fewer in the ideal eleven; across all Premier League teams on average, 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal starting eleven, with similar expected points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14], [11:44]). The headline at the end, "approximately 13% on average" fewer injuries, matches the ideal-eleven figure, not the 4.6% squad figure, and the speaker does not say which (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]). Compared with real coaches, the search model's selections were about 76% similar and the greedy model's about 82%; the presenters suggest managers face short-term pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43]). They also say real technical directors often decide for short-term gains over long-term athlete protection (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:48]); he introduces it with "We also found," but no data or survey of directors is shown (Inference: it is a belief or anecdote, not a result of the simulation).
**Why it works** — The speakers' explanation is that the search values future availability and the greedy rule does not. They give no mechanism beyond the injury model's workload dependence; see [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]. Inference: because both models use the same injury model to score the outcome, the comparison measures how the injury model's own risk estimates change selections, not real injuries.
**When to apply** — As an illustration of what a rest-rotation decision model might claim, and of the size of benefit a vendor or paper could be expected to show. Inference: a claim of fewer injuries from a model should come with the injury model's validation, which this talk gives only partly (log loss 0.16, Pearson 0.77; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]]).
**When NOT to apply** — Untested: all results are simulated from open data (StatsBomb 2017/18 and 2018/19 Premier League events, Transfermarkt injury history), with player load imputed and no club medical or training data (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [13:48], [17:53]). No club has used the recommendations, and the greedy comparison ran "for one season" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]; the caption does not name it, and the preceding model check used 2018/19), so it is a single simulated season. Substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). One league, professional soccer; do not apply the percentages to college football. Inference: rotation there is far more limited. One presenter introduces himself as the CEO and co-founder of a UK-based startup (K5a7C4b1Cwc [00:30]), so there is a commercial interest. The 13% versus 4.6% ambiguity above means the headline should be quoted with both figures.
**Example** — The speakers' own: Brighton, 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven at similar points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14]).

Auto-caption talk from 2017; the results were presented by a speaker with a sleep-lab affiliation, not as a peer-reviewed table. # About Half a Billion Dollars of MLB Salary Went to UCL Rehab, 2004 to 2014
**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]). (Untested: bare assertion, no method given.)
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]). (Untested: back-of-envelope, unadjusted.)
**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.
**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.
**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Inference: MLB dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.
**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).

# Simulated Result: Tree-Search Selection Cut Injuries at Similar Expected Points
**What it is** — The presenters compared their search-based selection with a greedy baseline that picks the team maximizing expected points for each match only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42], [10:12]). They ran thousands of simulations per season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:43], [11:14]). Reported: Brighton would have benefited most, with 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least, with 7.5% fewer in the ideal eleven; across all Premier League teams on average, 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal starting eleven, with similar expected points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14], [11:44]). The headline at the end, "approximately 13% on average" fewer injuries, matches the ideal-eleven figure, not the 4.6% squad figure, and the speaker does not say which (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]). Compared with real coaches, the search model's selections were about 76% similar and the greedy model's about 82%; the presenters suggest managers face short-term pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43]). They also say real technical directors often decide for short-term gains over long-term athlete protection (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:48]); he introduces it with "We also found," but no data or survey of directors is shown (Inference: it is a belief or anecdote, not a result of the simulation).
**Why it works** — The speakers' explanation is that the search values future availability and the greedy rule does not. They give no mechanism beyond the injury model's workload dependence; see [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]. Inference: because both models use the same injury model to score the outcome, the comparison measures how the injury model's own risk estimates change selections, not real injuries.
**When to apply** — As an illustration of what a rest-rotation decision model might claim, and of the size of benefit a vendor or paper could be expected to show. Inference: a claim of fewer injuries from a model should come with the injury model's validation, which this talk gives only partly (log loss 0.16, Pearson 0.77; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]]).
**When NOT to apply** — Untested: all results are simulated from open data (StatsBomb 2017/18 and 2018/19 Premier League events, Transfermarkt injury history), with player load imputed and no club medical or training data (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [13:48], [17:53]). No club has used the recommendations, and the greedy comparison ran "for one season" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]; the caption does not name it, and the preceding model check used 2018/19), so it is a single simulated season. Substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). One league, professional soccer; do not apply the percentages to college football. Inference: rotation there is far more limited. One presenter introduces himself as the CEO and co-founder of a UK-based startup (K5a7C4b1Cwc [00:30]), so there is a commercial interest. The 13% versus 4.6% ambiguity above means the headline should be quoted with both figures.
**Example** — The speakers' own: Brighton, 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven at similar points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14]).

=== claim--teammate-familiarity-improves-catch-and-shoot-shot-quality.md
# Passer-shooter pairs choose better shots the more catch-and-shoot attempts they share
**What it is** — Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver report that NBA passer-shooter pairs improve their shot selection as the pair accumulates catch-and-shoot attempts together. Taking a pair's value at 0% and following its first 200 catch-and-shoot attempts, the curve rises steeply: about 7% better shot selection in the first 50 attempts, then about another 4% up to 200 (o4rMbhsdk0I [09:43]). Players rarely get more than 200 such attempts in one season (o4rMbhsdk0I [09:43]). The pair does not reset to zero in the next season: the speaker says it starts about five percent above where they started from (paraphrase of auto-caption), below the end of the prior season, and by the end of season two it is better than at the end of season one (o4rMbhsdk0I [10:14]). The units of the 7% and 4% are not defined in the captions (the measure is expected points per shot from their shot-quality model, so these are most likely relative changes in expected points; Inference).
**Why it works** — The speakers show three measurable drivers of the better shots: shorter two-point attempts, lower pressure on the passer, and more open shots, with about a 4% decline in pressure score over the first 100 shots (o4rMbhsdk0I [10:47], [11:18], [11:48]). They read this as the passer finding the partner sooner, before the defense reacts (o4rMbhsdk0I [11:48]). They do not test why the pair learns; the mechanism of learning itself is not given.
**When to apply** — As a prior for how fast a newly formed pairing should improve: steep early, then slower, with partial carry-over across seasons. Inference: for a new football pairing (transfer quarterback with new receivers), treat the first weeks of numbers as the steep part of a curve rather than as the pair's level. Eric's baseline: new movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3 to 4 weeks of practice to become efficient (course team position, speaker unconfirmed, Inferred). The talk agrees in direction but measures attempts, not weeks, so the time scales are not comparable.
**When NOT to apply** — The analysis is on NBA catch-and-shoot attempts, though the speaker says the analysis is consistent across all shot attempts (o4rMbhsdk0I [07:38]). Context figures the speaker gives "just for some context" for the 2023-24 season (not the full analysis set): 1600 passer-shooter combinations with 10 to 50 catch-and-shoot attempts, averaging 1.12 points per attempt (o4rMbhsdk0I [07:08], [07:38]). The seasons in the regression are not stated; the model uses in-season and multiple-season counters (o4rMbhsdk0I [08:40]). The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb (o4rMbhsdk0I [17:27]), say the results are statistically significant but noisy (o4rMbhsdk0I [21:03]), and say pair-level results are noisy and biased because one person typically did most of the passing to a shooter (o4rMbhsdk0I [21:33]). The effect is stronger for catch-and-shoot than for all shot types (o4rMbhsdk0I [24:07]). No age, rookie or role adjustments were made (o4rMbhsdk0I [35:23]). Football pass plays per quarterback-receiver pair are far fewer than repeated catch-and-shoot attempts (Inference). Do not use the curve to grade or rank individual pairs.
**Example** — The speakers' own example is the 2020-21 Phoenix Suns (see [[case-study--phoenix-suns-chris-paul-familiarity-ramp]]).
=== claim--youth-specialization-survey-and-early-surgery.md
# Year-Round Youth Baseball: Arm Pain Is Common, Pressure to Play On Is Common
**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally gives early single-sport specialization and year-round play as the second reason UCL surgeries are not falling (z_6M5r7031A [06:10] to [07:10]). He says specialization before kids are skeletally mature is "causing a burnout" of muscles and tendons (z_6M5r7031A [07:10]).
- **Survey:** 200 healthy youth baseball players who were not complaining of pain, surveyed "when I was in residency in New York City." 75% admitted arm pain (z_6M5r7031A [07:10]). 25% had symptoms suggestive of a legitimate overuse injury, and 50% felt pressured to play despite admitting arm pain, by coaches and parents (z_6M5r7031A [07:41]).

23:**When NOT to apply** — Untested: unnamed studies, sample sizes not stated; the restriction is described as one week (J7smyg1Czik [06:12]), and the caption garble in the key sentence. Young healthy college students (the speaker does not say how many or of which sex) in laboratory conditions. Existing library: a 2026 review of testosterone in athletes notes that sleep loss and sleep-disordered breathing may contribute to impaired testosterone regulation, and that evidence for sleep extension or melatonin as testosterone-enhancing interventions is not established, so do not present this as a treatment effect. The "age 31" comparison (J7smyg1Czik [06:12]) is the speaker's illustration, not a finding the speaker cites. Do not use this to interpret an athlete's own lab values.
27:**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[claim--sleep-hours-predicted-injury-in-high-school-athletes]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lazarev-2026-testosterone-optimizing-strategies-in-athletes]] (partial tension on sleep as an intervention, not on the effect of loss).
== framework--wearable-validation-workflow.md
20:3. **Validate** the wearable against something you can trust, in her example hormone measures, using a survey that gives baseline information about the wearer and a diverse group of users (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:19] to [33:51]).
24:Her wider advice: use multiple wearables, validate against hormones, tweak the wearable, and ask questions over time (an7u-tVP5Xc [34:22]). Run it as a team: an endocrinologist, a sports physician, athlete input and a data analytics expert (an7u-tVP5Xc [29:14], [34:53] to [35:24]).
26:Background reasons she gives: sensors differ in what they measure and in validity, so "any wearable" data are "apples and oranges"; with no test against a gold standard "we're making a lot of assumptions" (an7u-tVP5Xc [20:32], [28:44] to [29:14]). She also raises data quality, health equity, algorithm bias, privacy and AI repeating errors with more confidence (an7u-tVP5Xc [29:44] to [31:17]).
28:**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is the validity point above: unvalidated devices carry unexamined assumptions. She gives no study showing the workflow itself improves results. Inference: the loop of step 5 treats a failed validation as information, not a wasted study.
32:**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is the speaker's flow, shown without a worked example or outcomes. Her reference standard is hormone testing for cycle-related wearables; other devices need their own trusted reference. It is a research workflow, not a procurement standard, and it does not say how much validation is enough. Her view that a team is needed is an institutional opinion; she leads an institute with philanthropic funding (an7u-tVP5Xc [25:40]).
34:**Example** — The speaker's own: a person who says "just plug in your wearable data," and her reply, "which wearable?" (an7u-tVP5Xc [28:44]).
== principle--asking-about-menstrual-status-is-not-testing-it.md
17:**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari," a sports doctor and endocrinologist) makes a measurement-validity point: asking someone about their cycle is "not the same as actually testing the hormone levels" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]). Someone on a birth control pill who reports a period has a withdrawal bleed while taking exogenous hormones, "not the same as having a natural menstrual cycle" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]). She asks researchers to use the same terminology: a withdrawal bleed from a pill, a naturally menstruating woman, and someone who ovulated and has a normal cycle are "all very different things" (an7u-tVP5Xc [20:01] to [20:32]). On her audit's gold, silver and bronze classification, she says gold and silver are where studies did some hormonal measurement and also reported and asked about status (an7u-tVP5Xc [19:00] to [19:30]); bronze is not defined in the transcript.
19:She also says it is not known whether training should change by cycle phase: "we don't know when it matters because we're not studying it enough," and it may be that nothing needs to change in someone without symptoms (an7u-tVP5Xc [08:43] to [09:14]).
21:**Why it works** — The speaker gives the definitional reasons above and no data. Inference: grouping athletes by self-reported phase mixes people with different hormonal states, which would blur any phase comparison, but she does not run this through.
25:**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: these are definitions and an expert's position, with no data or citations in the talk. It gives no training recommendation by phase; she says the evidence is missing (an7u-tVP5Xc [08:43]). It does not say how often hormone testing is needed or practical for a team. It is not a clinical guide for any individual.
27:**Example** — The speaker's own: an athlete says "I'm on my period" while taking a birth control pill; that is a withdrawal bleed on exogenous hormones, "not the same as having a natural menstrual cycle" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]). Inference: a study coding her as in a natural cycle phase would misclassify her.
